name: Band together
summary: Members of a set group (one unit type, or a few types that count one another) get better at their job while enough of them stand close together: in Command & Conquer: Generals each Chinese horde soldier fires half again as fast once at least four others of its group are near it. No single unit hands out the bonus; every member checks its own neighbours, so there is no leader to snipe, but thinning the crowd, splitting it or luring part of it away switches the bonus off for every member left short. Some versions add tiers as the crowd grows. It pushes a side to move as one tight blob, which is exactly what splash weapons and ambushes at chokepoints punish.
counterplay: Use splash: members bunch up to keep the bonus, so area weapons hit many at once; the Generals wiki names the Ranger's flash-bang grenades against massed Red Guards.
Pick off a few: each loss can drop the rest below the count, and the Generals wiki notes that losing a single Battlemaster can break the bonus for the others.
Split them: ambush the group at a chokepoint so it can't mass, or draw part of it away with a feint.
Make them string out: vehicle columns spread out when they fire at full range and lose the bonus, so fight them at long range where they can't stay packed.
Bring what the pack lacks: a blob of cheap rifle troops still has no answer to aircraft or tanks, and escorts that cover those gaps don't count toward the bonus.

other_examples.note: China's basic tank gets the same rate-of-fire bonus as the horde infantry, but only from other Battlemasters, in groups of five; the side-wide Nationalism upgrade raises it. The wiki lists what the bonus costs: a mass of tanks covers so much ground that only some can engage a target at once, losing one tank can break the bonus for the rest, ambushes at chokepoints stop the group from massing, and fitting in the anti-air and detector escorts the tanks need without losing the bonus is fiddly because the escorts move at other speeds. A column that opens fire at its longest reach also loosens its spacing, which drops the bonus.

sources.title: Horde Bonus, Command & Conquer Wiki
sources.note: Gives the group of five, the faster fire, the red star under horded units, the infantry mix that excludes Battlemasters and the spreading of vehicle columns.

other_examples.unit: Ork Waaagh! (Slugga Boy Squad and other Ork squads)
other_examples.note: Ork squads draw bonuses from massing, counted in mob value. With enough mob value in its own squad an Ork squad recovers morale and health faster; when enough Ork mob value gathers within a set radius, every Ork there becomes immune to morale damage; and once the side's population is high enough and a Pile O' Gunz stands, squads also gain a little speed and damage. The wiki's advice is to keep Slugga Boy squads at full size to raise their morale.

sources.title: Soulstorm/Slugga Boy Squad, Dawn of War Wiki

other_examples.game: extra:Total War: Warhammer II and III
other_examples.note: Most Skaven infantry and missile infantry carry a passive that gives better melee defence and leadership at the cost of some speed, but only while the unit keeps more than half its hit points. Here the pack is the unit's own regiment, so casualties that halve it switch the bonus off. Heroes and lords, monsters, monstrous infantry and artillery go without it.

sources.title: Strength in Numbers, Total War: Warhammer Wiki

shooter_analogues.note: Players who stay close to one another are in coherency, and the more teammates in it, the faster toughness, the bar that soaks damage before health, refills. Class auras and many talents reach only allies in coherency, such as a Psyker's damage bonus or a Veteran's ammo on killing special enemies, and those specials are more likely to go after players who wander off alone. Fatshark's notes for patch 1.10.6 say that some talents' toughness regeneration worked only while in coherency and out of combat, and swapped those talents for a bonus to all toughness gained.

sources.title: Chaos Undivided - How Teamwork is Crucial in Warhammer 40,000: Darktide, Level Infinite
sources.note: A teamwork guide on the news site of Tencent's Level Infinite label (December 2022, updated February 2024).

sources.title: Patch 1.10.6 - Patch Notes, Fatshark Forums
sources.note: The developer's announcement of February 2026; only its Hive Scum note about coherency is used.

player_translation.summary: A passive for cheap T1 cards that several teammates buy: while enough teammates on cards of the same group stand within a short radius, each of them fires faster, shown by a ring under every member. No one card gives the bonus, so the group plays as a pack, and the enemy answers with splash, picks and splits.
as_user: You buy a cheap soldier card with the group passive. Alone you are ordinary; with two or more teammates on cards of the same group close by, a ring lights under you and you fire much faster.
You win by moving as a pack: follow your squad, stay inside the radius and push together. A straggler loses the bonus, and as the group thins the others lose it too.
Cards of different types count toward each other when they share a group, as Red Guards and Tank Hunters do, so an anti-armour card can hide in a crowd of riflemen and keep the bonus going.
The blob is your weakness: when grenades or other splash weapons appear, spread out to the edge of the radius and kill the grenadier first.
as_target: You see a ring under every enemy who has the bonus, so you know which pack is dangerous and which straggler is weak.
Throw splash into the pack, snipe one member to drop the rest below the count, or pull a few apart with a feint; each member's ring goes out the moment it falls short.
Fight them where they can't mass, such as a chokepoint or a long sightline that makes them string out.
teammates: The group's team: three or four teammates on group cards move as one, which suits a squad of four; bots on the team count like players.
The enemy team: splash weapons and area denial are the hard counter, and a marksman who removes one member weakens all the others.
Escorts that don't share the group, such as an anti-air vehicle, can travel with the pack to cover its gaps but don't add to the count.
controls: No key: the bonus is a passive and uses the card's one passive slot.
Middle mouse, the universal ping, on a spot: 'group up here'.
The HUD shows how many group members are in range and points to the nearest one when you are out of it.
feedback: A coloured ring under every member while the bonus holds, with pips for the members who count; it flickers when one more loss would break it.
A faster, punchier firing sound while boosted, so both teams hear the difference.
Members of a mixed group share one ring colour, so enemies can tell which units count toward it.
changes_from_rts: Generals needs five horde soldiers together, which one player's army reaches easily. Teams of players drift apart, so the count drops to three, the radius grows, and bots count.
Generals lets soldiers who enter a building keep the bonus they had on entering. Here it works only on foot and outside, or it rewards camping inside.
Generals strengthens the bonus with side-wide upgrades such as Nationalism; with no side-wide research here, a stronger version would be a T2 variant instead.
A side in Generals masses dozens of cheap troops; a player card needs a usable base weapon too, so a player who drifts off the pack is weaker but not helpless.

team_play.notes: The purest swarm pattern: the bonus exists only while several players on cards of the same group move together, and the enemy must answer it with splash, marksmen or ambushes that split the pack.

notes: A radius check every few ticks that counts allies with the same group tag, cheap with a spatial grid.
A short grace time when a member leaves the radius, so the bonus doesn't flicker at the edge.
Group tags for mixed cards, and bots counted like players, decided by the server.
A ring and a count that read clearly from a top-down camera.
A big pack of cheap cards can snowball: half again the rate of fire, as in Generals, multiplied across many players. Cap the bonus and keep it on cheap T1 cards.
A strong pull toward blob play can make matches samey and force every team to bring splash; keep the bonus modest.
A count that suits a big team is out of reach in a small one; scale the count with team size, or the card is dead weight in small games.
The ring under each member and the count read easily from above.
Mixed groups need one shared ring colour, or enemies can't tell which units count.

variants.name: Horde fire
variants.summary: With enough members of its group nearby, each member fires faster; a loss that drops it below the count switches the bonus off. The basic version.
variants.seen_in: Generals Red Guard, Tank Hunter and Mini-Gunner horde bonus

variants.name: Close ranks
variants.summary: Standing close to more teammates makes shields or toughness refill faster, and the card's aura reaches only allies in range; a defensive version that rewards staying together without raising damage.

adds_strengths.why: With teammates of its group close by, its shield or toughness refills much faster, so a tight group outlasts a scattered one.

variants.name: Armoured pack
variants.summary: The vehicle version: only vehicles of the same card count, and the pack's footprint means only some of them can fire at one target at a time.

variants.name: Tiered mob
variants.summary: The bonus grows in steps: a small group recovers faster, a bigger crowd in range becomes immune to fear or suppression, and once the whole side is large (in Dawn of War, with a certain building standing) members also move and hit a little harder.
variants.seen_in: Dawn of War: Soulstorm Ork Waaagh!

variants.name: Intact squad
variants.summary: The bonus counts your own squad, not whoever stands nearby: it holds while more than half of the squad is alive, trading a little speed for better defence, and casualties switch it off.
variants.seen_in: Total War: Warhammer Skaven Strength in Numbers

adds_strengths.why: With enough teammates of its group close by it fires much faster, so a pack of cheap cards outguns a lone stronger unit.

adds_weaknesses.why: Alone or cut off from its pack it loses the bonus, so it is weak in small games and against enemies who pick off or split the group.

counters.why: A boosted pack of cheap cards overwhelms a single expensive unit that can only shoot one of them at a time, the numbers game the Generals wiki describes for massed Battlemasters.

countered_by.why: The bonus makes the pack bunch up, so area weapons hit many members at once; the Generals wiki names flash-bang grenades against massed Red Guards.
Picking off a single member can drop the rest below the count, as losing one Battlemaster can break the bonus for its group.

open_questions: How many teammates should the bonus need in teams of 2 to 24: three including yourself, or five as in Generals?
Should bots on the team count toward the group?
Which bonus fits best: faster fire as in Generals, faster toughness refill as in Darktide, or tiers as in Dawn of War?
Should cards of different types share a group, as Red Guards and Tank Hunters do, or should only identical cards count?

shooter_fit.reason: Simple and team-building, as Darktide's coherency shows, but players in a shooter drift apart and a big bonus invites blob play that splash weapons punish; it fits as a modest passive on cheap cards.
